objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will have recorded a short structured talk about online safety, using a clear thesis, supporting reasons, an example, and simple emphasis phrases.
materials: - Follow-on from previous lesson: OFD2, Student Book pp10-11 (Protecting Online Identity)

stages.stage_aim: To reconnect learners with the topic of online identity protection and set up the recording goal
stages.procedure:
- As Ss enter, tell them to sit with a partner from last lesson for a quick discussion. 'Tell your partner: one thing you remember about identity theft from last lesson. You have 30 seconds.'
- Take 2 rapid-fire answers from pairs.
- Announce today's goal: 'You're going to record a short talk about online safety — 60 seconds. One take. This is your baseline for the year.'
- Frame the purpose: 'This is a snapshot of where you are right now. Next time we record, you'll hear how much you've improved.'

stages.stage_aim: To revisit the talk structure from last lesson and introduce simple emphasis phrases learners can use to make their talks more powerful
stages.procedure:
- Display the 'Structure Your Talk' framework on the board:
  • Thesis: Say your main idea (e.g. 'Online safety is important for everyone.')
  • Reasons: Give 1–2 reasons (e.g. 'First, hackers can steal your personal information.')
  • Example: Share an example you know (e.g. 'For example, my friend’s account was hacked.')
- Remind Ss: 'We used this structure last lesson. Today you'll use it again, but you'll also make your talk stronger.'
- Introduce emphasis phrases in three groups:
  • Opening / stating importance: 'It’s really important to…', 'I want to say that…'
  • Giving strong advice: 'You should always…', 'You should never…'
  • Making your point stronger: 'The main thing is…', 'I strongly believe that…'
- Model each phrase with a simple example: 'It’s really important to use strong passwords.' Drill chorally (2 rounds) and individually (2–3 Ss).
- Ss note down 2–3 phrases they want to use in their talk.

stages.stage_aim: To give learners a quick low-stakes chance to practise using the emphasis phrases aloud before writing their full script
stages.procedure:
- 'Exercise A — Mini-talk. You have 30 seconds to talk about one thing you do to stay safe online. Use at least one emphasis phrase.'
- Ss prepare silently for 1 minute: think of their topic, pick one phrase.
- Ss deliver their mini-talk to their partner (not the whole class). Partner listens and counts the emphasis phrase used. (2 min)
- Switch roles: the other partner delivers their mini-talk while the first partner counts phrases. (2 min)

stages.stage_aim: To guide learners through writing a 60-second structured talk about online safety with thesis, reasons, example, and emphasis phrases
stages.procedure:
- Start an 8-minute countdown timer on the board.
- 'Write a 60-second talk about online safety. Use the structure from last lesson and include at least 2 emphasis phrases.'
- Display the script checklist on the board:
  ✅ Clear thesis — your main idea about online safety
  ✅ At least 1 reason to support your idea
  ✅ A real example from your life or someone you know
  ✅ At least 2 emphasis phrases from the lesson
  ✅ A short closing sentence
  ✅ 60 seconds when you speak it aloud
- Circulate and help Ss who are stuck. Remind them of the countdown at 4 min and 1 min. Push for natural language, not written-sounding sentences.

stages.stage_aim: To help learners practise their delivery and confirm their timing before the recording starts
stages.procedure:
- 'Three minutes to rehearse. Time yourself.'
- Round 1 (2 min): Ss practise their talk aloud with their script. Partner raises a hand when 60 seconds have passed so they know if they're on track.
- Round 2 (1 min): Ss practise again, this time trying to look up from the script and sound natural.
- Teacher moves between 2–3 Ss, giving quick coaching: 'Louder — project your voice.' 'You're at 45 seconds — you need more.' 'Good use of the emphasis phrase — keep it.'

stages.stage_aim: To capture each learner's baseline recording of a structured talk about online safety as a reference point for future progress
stages.procedure:
- Set up a recording device at the front. 'One take only. No restarts. This is your baseline.'
- 'When I call your name, come to the front, deliver your 60-second talk, and sit down. Everyone else — absolutely silent during recording.'
- Call Ss one at a time. Each delivers their 60-second talk. Teacher records without offering feedback, corrections, or gestures during the recording.
- Between Ss, call the next name immediately — no dead air, no commentary on the previous performance.
- With 18 Ss at 60 seconds each plus transitions, the 20-minute block fits comfortably at roughly 65–70 seconds per student. Stagger efficiently: call the next student up while the previous one is walking back.
- If all Ss finish early but time remains, any student who wants a second take may do one. If time runs short, remaining Ss record at the start of the next lesson.

stages.stage_aim: To encourage learners to reflect on the recording experience and recognise this baseline as the start of their progress
stages.procedure:
- Display two reflection prompts on the board: 'What was the hardest part?' and 'What went better than you expected?'
- 'Turn to your partner. Discuss these two questions for 60 seconds. No whole-class feedback — this is for you.'
- After 60 seconds, deliver the closing statement: 'That recording is your starting point. In a few months, you’ll listen back and see how far you’ve come. Well done today.'
- Dismiss.
